newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs Neurex hypertension drug.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs Neurex hypertension drug.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory committee Thursday voted 9-1 to recommend approval of Neurex Corp's fenoldopam (Corlopam) for use in hypertensive patients who cannot take oral medications, and 8-2 for patients who have severe, acute high blood pressure.
The panel said that it wanted Neurex to do a trial on how Corlopam, given by infusion, interacts with other medications, such as beta blockers, likely to be given in conjunction with it.
The FDA is not bound by its panels' advice, but usually follows it.
In 1994, Neurex licensed Corlopam from SmithKline Beecham PLC, which had previously applied for FDA approval.

Neurex reapplied in June 1996, attempting to address agency questions about dosing instructions and whether the drug worsens organ damage in patients with malignant hypertension, a condition that can lead to death.

Raymond Lipicky, director of FDA's Cardio-Renal Drugs Division, said that he still felt Neurex had not given physicians enough data on dosing. The panel also struggled with whether the company had given enough information.
"There may have to be some empirical decision-making by physicians," said panelist Michael Weber of Brookdale University Medical Center in Brooklyn, N.Y.

There was some concern also that Corlopam might contribute to a heart beat irregularity, but panelist John DiMarco of the University of Virginia, speaking for the committee, said, "I don't think this would be a major concern."

The potential market, according to Neurex, is 450,000 patients who require cardiac surgery each year in the United States, another 300,000 with post-operative hypertension, and 120,000 with so-called malignant hypertension. There are seven other drugs are already on the market for the indications.
Neurex CEO Paul Goddard said price would probably be close to analysts' estimates of $200-to-300 per patient.

Corlopam has been studied in 1,000 patients in 11 trials, mostly by SmithKline. Neurex says Corlopam is as effective, if not more so, than other available drugs. Overall in trials, diastolic blood pressure was reduced by 24-to-33 millimeters of mercury. In a study of severe hypertensives who required emergency treatment, 89 patients, mostly African American, were assigned to receive one of four doses of Corlopam, given over 24 hours. A placebo was not used because it was considered unethical, said Neurex. Blood pressure was measured at four hours; in the group receiving the highest dose, there was a significant decrease, Neurex said.

Neurex said the drug was safe, noting that the most frequent side effect was headache and flushing. There were 23 non-fatal serious adverse events, such as hypotension, and some heart rate irregularities, which resolved when therapy was stopped. There were 19 deaths among the 1,000 patients, but Neurex said that only three occurred while patients were taking the drug. And those did not seem to be related to Corlopam, Neurex said.
